content: Effective infection prevention and control measures are essential to minimize the risk of Mycobacterium tuberculosis transmission. These practices work by reducing the concentration of infectious droplet nuclei in the air and limiting the exposure of susceptible individuals to such aerosols. Globally, there are approximately 5 million new chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections annually. The transmission of HCV is most commonly associated with unsafe injection practices, inadequate infection control in healthcare settings, and the sharing of needles and syringes among people who inject drugs. In regions such as Central and East Asia, as well as North Africa and the Middle East, the prevalence of HCV remains significant. For hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, the primary modes of transmission globally are perinatal (mother-to-child) and horizontal (person-to-person) transmission during early childhood. However, HBV can also be transmitted through injecting drug use and high-risk sexual behaviors. The highest prevalence of HBV surface antigen (HBsAg) (>5%) is observed in sub-Saharan Africa and East Asia. Most individuals with chronic HBV infection were infected at birth or during early childhood, leading to high rates of chronic infection. Between 20% and 30% of individuals with chronic HBV infection develop complications, primarily cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. HIV and HCV co-infection is particularly prevalent in concentrated epidemic settings, such as among people who inject drugs in Central Asia and Eastern Europe, accounting for 27% of the global HIV and HCV burden. HIV and HCV share common transmission routes, and individuals living with HIV, especially those who inject drugs or are men who have sex with men, are at increased risk of acquiring HCV. In sub-Saharan Africa, HBV infection is predominantly acquired perinatally or during early childhood, meaning that most individuals have been infected with HBV for many years by the time they are exposed to HIV in adulthood. Liver disease caused by co-infection with HBV or HCV is an increasing cause of morbidity and mortality among people living with HIV, including those receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART). Co-infection with HIV typically results in more severe and progressive liver disease, with higher incidences of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and mortality. Therefore, individuals living with HIV are a priority group for early diagnosis of viral hepatitis co-infection and subsequent treatment. HCV-related liver disease progresses more rapidly in individuals co-infected with HIV and HCV compared to those solely infected with HCV. Even among individuals whose HIV infection is well-controlled with ART (evidenced by undetectable HIV viral loads), the risk of hepatic decompensation remains higher in co-infected individuals. Consequently, HCV treatment is a priority for people with HIV and HCV co-infection. A comprehensive approach includes prevention, testing for HBV and HCV, HBV vaccination, and treatment and care for individuals living with HIV who are co-infected with HBV and/or HCV. Testing for HBV and HCV infection is critical as it serves as the gateway to prevention and treatment services. Early identification of individuals with chronic HBV or HCV infection allows for timely care and treatment to prevent or delay the progression of liver disease. Testing also provides an opportunity to link individuals to interventions aimed at reducing transmission, such as counseling on risk behaviors, provision of sterile needles and syringes, and HBV vaccination. The 2017 WHO testing guidelines recommend targeted testing for individuals from populations most affected by HBV or HCV infection, including those with a history of exposure or high-risk behaviors. This includes all adults and adolescents living with HIV. Other priority groups include mobile and migrant populations from high-endemic countries, certain indigenous populations, people who inject drugs, individuals in prisons, men who have sex with men, sex workers, and healthcare workers. Routine testing is also recommended for pregnant women in antenatal care settings, with linkage to prevention, care, and treatment services. For individuals co-infected with HBV and HCV, there is a potential risk of HBV reactivation and worsening liver disease when initiating direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy for HCV. Therefore, testing for HBV infection and considering antiviral therapy is recommended before starting DAA treatment. For people living with HIV, ART regimens containing tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) with lamivudine (3TC) or emtricitabine (FTC) should be initiated prior to starting DAA therapy. The WHO guidelines recommend using a single quality-assured serological test to detect HBsAg and HCV antibodies. Rapid diagnostic tests or laboratory-based immunoassays can be used, provided they meet minimum performance standards. Following a reactive HCV antibody test, a quantitative or qualitative RNA nucleic acid test (NAT) is recommended to confirm viremia. Alternatively, detecting HCV core antigen may be considered if the assay has comparable sensitivity to NAT technologies. For HCV treatment, outcomes with DAA therapy are comparable for individuals co-infected with HIV and HCV to those solely infected with HCV. However, drug-drug interactions between HIV and HCV medications must be carefully managed. Prescribers are advised to consult resources such as the University of Liverpool’s hepatitis drug interaction database to ensure safe prescribing practices. Universal infant and perinatal HBV vaccination remains the cornerstone strategy for preventing mother-to-child transmission and controlling the HBV epidemic. Despite significant progress in infant vaccination coverage, the implementation of HBV birth-dose vaccination remains suboptimal in many countries. Adults living with HIV are at higher risk of HBV infection, and all newly diagnosed individuals with HIV should be screened for HBsAg and anti-HBs to identify those with chronic HBV infection and to offer vaccination if non-immune. People living with HIV may have a reduced response to the HBV vaccine, particularly those with low CD4 cell counts. A schedule using four double doses (40 µg) of the vaccine may provide better protection than the standard three-dose schedule. In the absence of treatment, HIV co-infection accelerates the progression of HBV-related liver disease, including cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, and increases liver-related mortality. Therefore, all individuals co-infected with HIV and HBV should receive a TDF-based ART regimen in combination with 3TC or FTC, regardless of disease stage or HBV DNA levels. Abrupt discontinuation of TDF or 3TC can lead to HBV reactivation, hepatic flares, and, in rare cases, hepatic decompensation. If ART regimens need to be changed due to HIV drug resistance or toxicity, TDF with 3TC or FTC should be continued alongside the new antiretroviral drugs. Routine testing of pregnant women for HIV, HBV, and syphilis is recommended, with all infants receiving their first dose of the HBV vaccine within 24 hours of birth.
